accroche: In 1913, a 35-year-old psychologist writes that consciousness no longer has a place in psychology. Many of his colleagues never got over the sentence.
contenu_vulgarise:
In March 1913, in the journal Psychological Review, John B. Watson opens his article with a sentence that serves as a program: “Psychology as the behaviorist views it is a purely objective experimental branch of natural science.” Psychology, he says, must become a science as objective as physics or chemistry. To get there, he proposes to throw overboard what had until then occupied the center of the discipline: consciousness.

Watson comes from comparative psychology, where he worked on rats and monkeys, for which introspection simply makes no sense. Making this animal tradition coexist with the human one, founded on inner testimony, seems impossible to him as long as they rest on incompatible methods. His solution is not to set aside a separate box for animals, but to align the study of humans with that of animals.

## What Watson Rejects

Introspection, the leading method of psychology at the time, consisted in asking trained subjects to describe their own sensations, mental images, or feelings. Watson judges it unusable: it forms, in his words, “no essential part of its methods.” He faults the discipline for systematically attacking the observer who reports his impressions rather than the experimental setup that provokes them: “the attack is made upon the observer and not upon the experimental setting.” The central concepts of introspection, sensation, feeling, image, are for him defined in no way that would let two laboratories agree. He demands the abandonment of “all reference to consciousness.”

What he keeps, in its place, is what can be observed from the outside: a stimulus, a response, and the regularities that habit establishes between the two. He wants to treat the data on humans and on animals on the same plane, with methods of study comparable to those already in use in animal psychology laboratories.

## What This Shifts

The text describes no new experiment. It reclassifies what counts as scientific data: what a subject says he feels goes out of the field, what can be observed and repeated comes in. The reaction does not take long. Edward Titchener, leader of structuralist introspection, publishes the very next year a reply in which he grants Watson his definition of psychology as an objective science, but refuses to let it exclude consciousness as the researcher's mere working tool. The debate opened in 1913 will run through the whole century: cognitive psychology, in the 1950s, will return to study what happens between the stimulus and the response, the box that Watson had wanted to leave closed.

carte.punch: In 1913, a psychologist writes that consciousness no longer has a place in science.
carte.idee: In Psychological Review, John Watson opens his article by defining psychology as a purely objective branch of the natural sciences, with no reference to consciousness or introspection. The article reports no experiment: it redefines what counts as scientific evidence.

pour_aller_plus_loin.note: Places the 1913 manifesto in the history of behaviorism, through to its cognitivist critics.

quiz.question: What does Watson mainly fault introspection for, in his 1913 manifesto?
choix: That it takes too much of the experimental subjects' time to be practicable in the laboratory
That it works well in animals but not in humans, which rules out any comparison
That it was invented by philosophers and not by psychologists trained in the natural sciences
That it rests on concepts defined in no way that would let laboratories agree
quiz.explication: Watson does not fault introspection for its slowness or its philosophical origin: he judges that its central concepts, sensation, feeling, image, are defined in no way that would let two laboratories agree on what they observe. That is why he demands the abandonment of all reference to consciousness.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Where does Watson come from when he writes this manifesto in 1913?
choix: From medical physiology, where he studied human reflexes
From comparative psychology, where he worked on rats and monkeys
From psychoanalysis, from which he was trying to break away
From philosophy, where he taught logic
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Watson comes from comparative psychology, where he worked on rats and monkeys, for which introspection makes no sense; this is what leads him to align the study of humans with that of animals.

quiz_supplementaire.question: How does Titchener react to Watson's article, the very next year?
choix: He entirely rejects the idea of an objective psychology
He approves without reservation the total abandonment of introspection
He ignores the article, which will be discussed only decades later
He accepts the objective definition, but refuses to exclude consciousness
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Titchener, leader of structuralist introspection, grants Watson his definition of psychology as an objective science, but refuses to let it exclude consciousness as the researcher's working tool.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does Watson keep, in place of introspection, to found his psychology?
choix: Laboratory tests timed to the tenth of a second
Physiological measurements of the central nervous system
The stimulus, the response, and the regularities that habit establishes
The detailed reports that subjects give of their sensations
quiz_supplementaire.explication: In place of introspection, Watson keeps what can be observed from the outside: a stimulus, a response, and the regularities that habit establishes between the two.
